source: Verma (2026) Solver-Hard Is Not Model-Hard: A Hardness-Controlled Diagnostic for LLM Constraint Reasoning
finding: Gap 4 and 10. Formulas matched on clause density and width but very different in CDCL proof cost (expander-Tseitin vs ladder-Tseitin) do not order LLM accuracy. Density and solver hardness are confounded in random 3-SAT, so earlier easy-hard-easy LLM curves may partly reflect density as a surface cue.
numbers: Glucose mean-conflict ratio expander/ladder grows 3.3x, 3.5x, 3.6x, 10.2x, 28.5x, 51.4x over six size bins; median conflicts about 5,550 vs 117 at about 60 variables. 243 instances per model. Accuracy gap ladder minus expander: Llama 3.3 70B +20 points (p=.015), Llama 4 Maverick -32 (p<.001), Mistral Large 3 +17 (p=.060); pooled +1.7 (p=.74). Correctness vs conflict count r=+0.15 (wrong sign).
limits: Three instruct models at temperature 0; a fourth (gpt-oss-120b) abstained on 189/243 and was excluded; no frontier reasoning model in the main accuracy test. Author says it bounds density and the conflict proxy, not all hardness.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a single hardness proxy (clause ratio or solver conflicts) to predict where the agent fails. Measure failure per family on our own items.

source: Verma (2026) Solver-Hard Is Not Model-Hard: A Hardness-Controlled Diagnostic for LLM Constraint Reasoning (pre-registered token-spend extension)
finding: Gap 4. Failure is partly a token-budget effect. At a 16,384-token cap a reasoning model hit the cap on every non-abstained row of the solver-easiest UNSAT family (random UNSAT, density 6) and got almost none right, while it solved the satisfiable control.
numbers: At 16k: all 28 non-abstained random-UNSAT rows reached the cap, accuracy .036; satisfiable control 1.00. 45/171 rows (26.3%) censored under a post-hoc rule (0/171 under the literal finish_reason flag). Spend vs conflict proxy raw correlation .33 becomes -.01 after length control. At 32k the C1 gap is absent. Models: Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B plus three instruct models.
limits: One reasoning model family; token counts are provider-reported; author says this does not show allocation inefficiency because no paired effort intervention was run.
agent_relevance: Budget exhaustion on UNSAT is a real failure mode. The scaffold needs an explicit stop-and-switch rule (hand to a code solver or abstain) before the cap, not more thinking.

source: Verma (2026) Solver-Hard Is Not Model-Hard: A Hardness-Controlled Diagnostic for LLM Constraint Reasoning (proof-preserving relabel and SAT control)
finding: Gap 10. Surface changes that keep the proof structure change accuracy a lot for some models, so verdicts depend on surface form. Satisfiable pigeonhole lookalikes raise the false-UNSAT rate for one model.
numbers: Relabelling lowers accuracy in all five clusters for one model (mean -93 points) but not another. False-UNSAT rate on satisfiable pigeonhole lookalikes .188 vs .021 for random SAT, 48 instances per family (Llama 3.3, +16.7 points, p=.0075); Llama 4 only +2.1. Pre-set gate (25 points in at least 2 of 5 models) not met.
limits: Small panel; only two completed models entered the SAT control.
agent_relevance: Paired-twin tests (same logic, new surface) are a cheap way to detect shortcuts. Add them to S4 TEST checks on SAT-like items.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Know Your Limits: On the Faithfulness of LLMs as Solvers and Autoformalizers in Legal Reasoning
finding: Gap 3. Autoformalisation to FOL plus Z3 on a re-annotated ContractNLI subset is the bottleneck. Letting the LLM 'run the solver' scores higher than the real solver, because the LLM adds unstated assumptions (scope laundering).
numbers: Accuracy (Simple / Structured / LLM-FR / Solver-FR): Claude 63.1/53.2/83.0/74.5; Deepseek 68.4/62.2/64.2/45.3; GPT 66.0/58.8/65.3/60.3; Qwen 65.1/61.5/69.1/48.3; Llama 55.9/40.0/58.6/42.1. Majority-class baseline 48%. Scope laundering rate from 15.3% (GPT) to 52.5% (Qwen; 28.6% excluding invalid inputs).
limits: Legal NLI, not SAT; five LLMs; strict formal entailment differs from legal reading, so low solver accuracy partly reflects missing premises, not only translation errors.
agent_relevance: Translation loss is large: real-solver accuracy fell below plain LLM classification for 4 of 5 models. A faithful-formalisation check is needed; 'about 100%' translate-and-solve results hold only on clean CNF tasks.

source: Sun and Meel (2026) SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
finding: Gaps 2 and 3. On a synthetic solver-tool benchmark (525 test items) current frontier models without training score 92-93%, and a small model needs SFT plus a logic-equivalence reward to use solvers faithfully. Without the equivalence reward, answers look right but the encoded formulas often are not equivalent to the problem.
numbers: In-domain Avg@8: GPT-5.6 Luna 92.0, Claude Sonnet 5 93.0, Claude Haiku 4.5 56.0, Qwen3.5-9B base 14.1, Qwen3.5-4B base 19.8. Qwen3.5-9B after SAT-RL 97.2 (sd 0.8), equivalence rate 94.0 (sd 1.7); without equivalence reward 91.2 accuracy but 80.6 equivalence (reward hacking, for example importing z3 and printing); without SFT 54.9. Out-of-domain Enigmata (1,901 items): Qwen3.5-9B 33.9 to 59.9 with SAT-RL, ReTool 47.9.
limits: Training paper, not a prompt-only scaffold; the benchmark is the authors' own synthetic set; text extraction of the out-of-domain table was partly garbled so only these OOD figures are used.
agent_relevance: The gap between answer accuracy and formula equivalence (91.2 vs 80.6) shows answer-only checks hide bad formalisation. Check the formalisation against the problem, not only the final label.

source: Luo et al. (2026) Bridging LLMs and SAT Solving: Automated Evolution of High-Performance Heuristics (AESAT)
finding: Gap 8. LLM-evolved heuristics for Kissat 4.0.2 MAB give small gains on held-out SAT Competition sets. Training used only 60 instances from the 2024 set. About 46% of functions that beat the baseline on training also beat it on the full sets.
numbers: Total solved over SAT Competition 2022-2025: Base MAB 1269, Kissat 4.0.2 1272, evolved UCB variants 1281 / 1287 / 1291, BumpInc 1272. 2025: Base MAB 335, best evolved 341, Kissat 330. 2024 PAR2: base 2139 vs 1883-2056 for the three UCB variants. Cost about 0.50 USD per returned function (30-40 hours) vs 20,000 USD for SATLUTION. Best training gain 36.6% on the 60 training instances, far above the full-set gain.
limits: Held-out means other competition years and the full 2024 set (which contains the training instances); no equal-budget parameter-tuning baseline; author-run hardware.
agent_relevance: Held-out gain (about 1-2% more solved) is far smaller than the training gain (36.6%). Selection on a small training set overstates. Keep a held-out check for any self-improved prompt or heuristic.

source: Luo et al. (2026) AESAT: competition result
finding: Gap 8. The paper states AE-Kissat-MAB won the main track and the SAT track of the 2025 SAT Competition by a wide margin, and AE-Kissat with BumpInc won silver in the main track. Official ranking on hidden instances is the strongest outside check on LLM-evolved solvers so far.
numbers: Claim in abstract and text; the BumpInc variant solved more UNSAT than Kissat-public in the competition. Table 1 in the paper shows only 3-6 instance differences per year between variants and baselines on the authors' runs.
limits: Self-reported in the paper; competition result tables not opened by me. SATLUTION (file c, 2509.07367) also claimed top results, so the claims overlap.
agent_relevance: Competition validation (hidden instances, equal time) is the standard to require. Template for judging scaffold changes.

source: Wang, Seggoju, Paschke (2026) Empirical Analysis of Chain-of-Thought and Solver-Augmented LLMs for Deductive Reasoning
finding: Gap 2. For current models (Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-5, DeepSeek-Reasoner) the solver-augmented pipeline gains under 1% over zero-shot CoT on ProofWriter, PrOntoQA and LogicalDeduction, which are near ceiling. On synthetic deep problems solver augmentation retains more accuracy.
numbers: GPT-5 ProofWriter CoT 98.60 vs solver 98.66 (+0.06); PrOntoQA 100 vs 100; LogicalDeduction 100.00 vs 99.56 (-0.44); average -0.13. DeepSeek-Reasoner ProofWriter 96.87 vs 98.61 (+1.74), LogicalDeduction 100 vs 99.33. Synthetic 14-17 step depth: solver retains 76.7% of accuracy vs 62.2% for CoT. Qwen3 14-32B near GPT-5 once they emit valid FOL; small DeepSeek-R1 distills often fail to produce formalisations.
limits: Not LSAT, BoardgameQA or GSM-SYS, so it does not replicate SatLM directly; benchmarks near ceiling; single-pass protocol; no token accounting.
agent_relevance: For strong reasoning models the SatLM-style gain mostly disappears on easy deduction. Expect a gain only on deep or hard-to-verify items. Delegate to a solver selectively.

source: Zhao et al. (2026, v2) SATQuest: A Verifier for Logical Reasoning Evaluation and Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of LLMs
finding: Gaps 4, 6, 9. Five SAT task types (decision, search, MaxSAT, minimal correction set, minimal unsatisfiable subset) in four formats; accuracy falls with solver-measured complexity. Models often fabricate solver calls or invent shortcut paths on hard items.
numbers: Overall accuracy (figure values): o3-mini 0.56, DeepSeek-R1 0.42, QwQ-32B 0.40, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 0.36, GPT-4.1 0.26, DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.18, R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 0.08, Qwen2.5-32B 0.07, Qwen2.5-7B 0.06. The prose lists GPT-4.1 0.38 and V3 0.36, which disagrees with the figure. For o3-mini on MCS and MUS tasks, response length decreases at high complexity, read by the authors as abandoning full reasoning. MCS and MUS are the hardest types.
limits: Figure vs prose mismatch; per-task cells not transcribed; different benchmark from SATBench so UNSAT-hardest is only partly comparable. Graded by PySAT: answers checked, traces not.
agent_relevance: A minimal unsatisfiable subset is a checkable UNSAT certificate and models do poorly at producing it. A checker can validate it cheaply; whether proof-style prompting helps (gap 9) remains untested.

source: Zhao et al. (2026, v2) SATQuest: format and reasoning style
finding: Gap 6. DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B reason directly in the DIMACS clause list instead of translating to a math form, which the authors link to semantic drift: conflating clauses and tracking many assignments at once. This is the authors' qualitative reading of traces.
numbers: Accuracy by format: highest for Math, then DIMACS, with Story lowest for most models; o3-mini is stable across formats. No counts of unit-propagation or backtracking events.
limits: Case-study observation, not an audited trace study. No test of DPLL-likeness vs local search.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. A trace audit with a script labelling propagate, decide and backtrack events is still unrun. We should run one.

source: Pan et al. (2025) Can Transformers Reason Logically? A Study in SAT Solving
finding: Gap 6. A hand-built transformer with chain-of-thought provably mimics DPLL backtracking and unit propagation; trained models learn it in distribution but not at longer lengths.
numbers: Search summary only; agrees with earlier entries in files a and c (99.8%+ in distribution; full trace 86.06% on harder rows).
agent_relevance: Shows DPLL is expressible in a transformer trace, not that off-the-shelf models use it.

source: FSTA 2026 proceedings: trace learning of unit propagation, conflict analysis and solver loop (title not captured)
finding: Gap 6 and 9. A 2026 paper trains models on solver traces (unit propagation, conflict analysis, main loop) and reports exact-match scores on out-of-distribution instances.
numbers: Web search summary only: mixed-training Solve 0.9711 and Conflict Analysis 0.7315 on OOD instances vs 0.9962 in distribution; OOD instances show about 2x call counts.
limits: Title, authors and URL not captured; not opened. Do not cite without finding the paper.

finding: No study found that tests a prompt-only scaffold (code unit propagation, explicit decide and backtrack trace, certificate check) against plain CoT and best-of-N at equal tokens on random 3-SAT (gap 1). None found for forced substitution checks of a claimed assignment in a fresh run (gap 5). None found on an LBD-like score for agent memory (gap 7).
numbers: About 12 arXiv API queries (mostly empty responses) and 6 web searches. Nothing matching.

source: SATBench judge design as reported by a search summary (arXiv 2505.14615)
finding: Gap 5 and 9. Search summary says SATBench's judge checks each clause against the model's claimed assignment (verification) and compares an UNSAT trace with a solver core. So checks exist in the grader but not as an in-loop forced check by the model.
numbers: SATBench hard: SAT 66.7% vs UNSAT 39.3% on average (already confirmed in files a and b).
limits: Snippet-level; the fresh-run question for the 60.4/73.2% correction effect is not resolved.
agent_relevance: Substituting a claimed assignment is a cheap code check; its effect on satisfiability bias remains untested by any paper found.
